subject: Number theory
title: Milne’s rationality conjecture and algebraic specialization
plain_explanation: Abelian varieties are higher-dimensional cousins of the doughnut, cut out by polynomial equations. They carry special "Hodge classes" that should come from real algebraic shapes inside them. Milne predicted that if you reduce the equations modulo a prime and measure these classes with any of the standard measuring tools (cohomology theories), you always get the same rational number. This proves it, and with result 032 shows each such class is one genuine algebraic shape in all those settings at once.

subject: Number theory
title: The full BSD formula from low Selmer corank
plain_explanation: Elliptic curves are equations like y² = x³ + ax + b. The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer (BSD) conjecture, a Millennium Prize problem, predicts how many rational solutions a curve has (its "rank") and gives an exact formula linking them to an L-function. This proves the full exact formula whenever a computable approximation (the Selmer group) says the rank is 0 or 1, and, with result 006, for "almost all" twisted versions of every curve. Bonus: every prime ℓ ≡ 4, 7, 8 (mod 9) is a sum of two rational cubes (Sylvester's old question). Ranks 2 and higher are not covered, so the Millennium problem itself is still open.

subject: Number theory
title: The quasi-Riemann hypothesis
plain_explanation: The Riemann Hypothesis says the important zeros of the zeta function all lie on the line Re s = 1/2. Until now nobody could even prove that a strip like Re s > 0.99 is free of zeros. This claims no zero has real part above 7/8 (for zeta and every Dirichlet L-function), which would sharply improve how precisely we can count primes. It also rules out "Landau–Siegel zeros", a long-feared kind of exceptional zero. Not the full Riemann Hypothesis, but by far the largest step toward it. OpenAI says this work did not follow its standard fixed procedure, and the 11/12 write-up was edited by humans.

subject: Number theory
title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over ℚ
plain_explanation: Hilbert's 10th problem asked for an algorithm that decides whether a polynomial equation has whole-number solutions; in 1970 that was shown to be impossible. The same question for fractions (rational solutions) stayed open for over 50 years. This proves no such algorithm exists for rational solutions either.

subject: Number theory
title: Irrationality of Catalan’s constant
plain_explanation: Catalan's constant G = 1 − 1/9 + 1/25 − 1/49 + … ≈ 0.91597. This proves G is irrational (not a fraction), a famous open question about one of the most natural constants in analysis.

subject: Number theory
title: Goldfeld’s conjecture: densities and mean analytic rank
plain_explanation: Take one elliptic curve and "twist" it by every square-free number d. Goldfeld conjectured that half of the twists have rank 0, half have rank 1, and higher ranks are negligible, so the average rank is 1/2. This proves it for every elliptic curve over the rationals.

subject: Number theory
title: Ordinary two-point correlations and the corrected Elliott conjecture
plain_explanation: The Liouville function λ(n) is +1 or −1 depending on whether n has an even or odd number of prime factors, and it is believed to behave like fair coin flips. Chowla's conjecture says it has no correlations: knowing λ(n) tells you nothing about λ(n+h). This proves the two-point version (pairs of values) with an explicit rate, and a more general version for other multiplicative functions.
quant_note: It is the same question you ask of returns: "does today's sign predict tomorrow's?" The lesson is that a completely deterministic rule can produce up/down sequences whose lag correlations average out to zero. Passing a lag-correlation test is not proof of randomness, and one lag looking "significant" is not proof of an edge. There is no tool to lift directly.

subject: Number theory
title: The Deligne–Drinfeld conjecture
plain_explanation: The Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra is a symmetry structure tied to multiple zeta values, the sums that link number theory, knot theory and quantum algebra. Deligne and Drinfeld predicted it is "free", with exactly one building block in each odd weight 3, 5, 7, …. This proves it, giving a clean description of a central object.

subject: Number theory
title: Function-field reconstruction from Milnor K-theory and Galois data
plain_explanation: A field of functions in two or more variables can be rebuilt completely from a small algebraic "fingerprint": its Milnor K-theory mod ℓ, or certain Galois-symmetry data (Bogomolov–Pop). It is like reconstructing an object from a few of its shadows.

subject: Number theory
title: Unrestricted pro-modularity at the prime two
plain_explanation: Galois representations encode the hidden symmetries of solutions to polynomial equations. "Modularity" means they come from modular forms, which are extremely symmetric functions; this is the bridge used to prove Fermat's Last Theorem. The prime 2 has always been the hardest case. This proves every suitable 2-adic two-dimensional representation is (pro-)modular, and the 2-adic Fontaine–Mazur conjecture without the usual extra conditions.

subject: Number theory
title: Prime-factor statistics of p-1
plain_explanation: Take a random prime p and look at the prime factors of p − 1. This proves their relative sizes follow the same random "stick-breaking" law (Poisson–Dirichlet) as the factors of a random whole number, settling the Ford–Konyagin–Luca conjecture. It also shows that some numbers are the totient φ(m) of more than n^(1−ε) different integers m.

subject: Number theory
title: Independent largest prime factors of consecutive integers
plain_explanation: Erdős and Pomerance asked whether the largest prime factors of n and n + 1 are independent of each other. This proves they are in the limit, so the largest prime factor of n + 1 is bigger than that of n exactly half the time.

subject: Number theory
title: Ostmann’s inverse Goldbach conjecture
plain_explanation: Could the primes, after changing finitely many of them, be written as all sums a + b from two sets A and B that each have at least two elements? Ostmann conjectured not. This proves the primes are "additively indecomposable".

subject: Number theory
title: Restricted geometric Langlands, global Arthur enhancements, and generic Ramanujan
plain_explanation: Geometric Langlands is a grand dictionary linking geometry over curves to representation theory. This family proves the "restricted" version over curves in positive characteristic (under stated conditions), proves Ramanujan-type bounds (eigenvalues as small as theory allows) for certain automorphic forms over function fields, and builds "Arthur enhancements" assuming a stated decomposition. With 8 papers it is one of the largest families.

subject: Number theory
title: Torus-packet equidistribution in prime, quartic, and sextic degrees
plain_explanation: Certain arithmetic orbits ("torus packets") built from number fields are shown to spread out perfectly evenly in their space as the field grows, with no mass escaping to infinity. This covers prime degree at least five, and quartic and sextic fields.

subject: Number theory
title: Zilber–Pink in abelian varieties and the Siegel threefold
plain_explanation: Zilber–Pink is about "unlikely intersections": a shape should meet special sub-shapes more often than dimension-counting predicts only in finitely many structured ways. This proves the full abelian-variety version over algebraic numbers, and the curve case in the Siegel modular threefold A₂.

subject: Number theory
title: The irrationality exponent of π is 2
plain_explanation: How well can π be approximated by fractions? This proves "no better than a typical number": for any ε > 0, |π − p/q| ≥ q^(−2−ε) once q is large. It also proves that the Flint Hills series Σ 1/(n³ sin² n) converges, a notorious open problem. The Lean check covers the exponent statement but not the series.

subject: Number theory
title: The Margulis–Platonov conjecture over global fields
plain_explanation: For arithmetic groups (for example matrix groups over number fields), the Margulis–Platonov conjecture describes all of their normal subgroups: they are controlled by finitely many local pieces. This proves it over every global field, including characteristic-2 function fields.

subject: Number theory
title: The local p-adic section conjecture and global consequences
plain_explanation: Grothendieck's section conjecture says the rational points on a curve of genus at least two can be read off from the symmetries of its fundamental group. This proves the local p-adic version for all such curves, and the global version over ℚ for the modular curves X₀(N) and X₁(N).

subject: Number theory
title: Squarefree quartics and power-free polynomial values
plain_explanation: For an irreducible degree-4 polynomial f with integer coefficients, how often is f(n) squarefree (not divisible by any square bigger than 1)? This proves it happens with exactly the predicted positive frequency. Similar results hold up to degree 8, so with earlier work every degree from 4 up is now covered.

subject: Number theory
title: A quadratic bound for Jacobsthal’s function
plain_explanation: How long can a run of consecutive integers be if every one of them shares a factor with a number that has k prime factors? This proves every run of C·k² consecutive integers contains one that shares no factor, a clean quadratic bound with no logarithmic loss.

subject: Number theory
title: The weak inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture
plain_explanation: This result is about approximating numbers by fractions when the target is shifted by a fixed amount γ. It proves the weak inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture: if a natural series diverges, then almost every number has infinitely many good shifted approximations.

subject: Number theory
title: Patterson's first moment for cubic Gauss sums
plain_explanation: Cubic Gauss sums are special sums built from cube roots of unity. Patterson predicted their average over primes has a main term of size X^(5/6)/log X. This proves it without any unproven assumptions.

subject: Number theory
title: An asymptotic formula for the number of totients
plain_explanation: How many different values does Euler's totient function φ take up to x? This gives a precise asymptotic formula, and answers Erdős and Hall's question by showing V(cx)/V(x) → c.

subject: Number theory
title: Short Egyptian fractions
plain_explanation: Every fraction a/b can be written as a sum of distinct unit fractions (1/n), the Egyptian way. Erdős asked how few are needed. The answer is on the order of log log b, and that is the best possible.

subject: Number theory
title: Positive lower density of large prime gaps
plain_explanation: Gaps between consecutive primes are about log p on average. This proves that, for any fixed C, a positive proportion of gaps are bigger than C·log p, answering a question of Erdős and Prachar.

subject: Number theory
title: Potential integral density on curve character varieties
plain_explanation: "Character varieties" list all the ways to represent a curve's fundamental group by matrices. This proves that points with integer-like coordinates (from one number field) fill them densely, answering Litt's question in the SL_r curve case.

subject: Number theory
title: Uniformly bounded components of Gaussian-prime graphs
plain_explanation: Gaussian primes are the primes in the grid of complex integers a + bi. The "Gaussian moat" problem asks whether you can walk off to infinity stepping only on Gaussian primes, with every step shorter than some fixed length. This proves you cannot: for every step size you are trapped on a finite island.

subject: Number theory
title: Primitive roots for every admissible integer base
plain_explanation: Artin's 1927 conjecture says any integer a that is not −1 or a perfect square is a primitive root (it generates every nonzero remainder) modulo infinitely many primes. Until now this was known only assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This proves it unconditionally, with a lower bound on how many such primes exist.

subject: Number theory
title: Modularity of elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields
plain_explanation: Modularity, the key ingredient in the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, is proven for every elliptic curve over every imaginary quadratic field, such as ℚ(i).

subject: Number theory
title: Uchida’s conjecture for open homomorphisms of Galois groups
plain_explanation: Uchida's conjecture says maps between certain Galois groups of number fields always come from actual embeddings of the fields. This proves it with no extra restrictions.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: The rational Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties
status: 3 companion papers withdrawn Oct 7; non-standard procedure
plain_explanation: The Hodge conjecture, a Millennium Prize problem, says certain topological classes on algebraic varieties come from actual algebraic sub-shapes. This proves it for CM abelian varieties (a highly symmetric family) in every dimension. Through Milne's theorems, it also gives the Tate conjecture for abelian varieties over finite fields. It is not the full Hodge conjecture. On Oct 7 OpenAI withdrew three companion papers (on K3 surfaces and abelian eightfolds) after a sign error was found.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Iitaka subadditivity, variation, and logarithmic additivity
plain_explanation: Kodaira dimension measures how "rich" a geometric space is in functions and forms. Iitaka's subadditivity says that when a space is fibred over a base, its richness is at least that of the fibre plus the base. This proves the orbifold and logarithmic versions conjectured by Campana and Popa.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Log abundance for compact Kähler spaces under logarithmic Iitaka subadditivity
plain_explanation: Abundance is a central conjecture of the minimal model program, the long project of classifying algebraic shapes. Using result 033, this proves log abundance for compact Kähler spaces and in characteristic zero, plus effective and uniform versions (14 papers). Several papers were revised on Oct 7 to repair positivity and contraction arguments.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Log-canonical threefold abundance in numerical dimension one
plain_explanation: This proves abundance for three-dimensional log canonical pairs in characteristic p > 3 when the "numerical dimension" is one. It is part of the shape-classification program in positive characteristic.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Numerical semiampleness and generalized minimal models
plain_explanation: These are technical pillars of the classification program: numerical semiampleness of nef adjoint classes, and existence of minimal models or Mori fibre spaces for generalized log canonical pairs. One paper was revised on Oct 7.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: The ordinary-double-point volume gap
plain_explanation: Singular points can be scored by a "normalized volume". This proves that the simplest singularity, the ordinary double point (like the tip of the cone x² + y² + z² = 0), has the largest volume among all singular points: a sharp gap in every dimension.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Fujita’s freeness conjecture
plain_explanation: Fujita's 1985 freeness conjecture says that on an n-dimensional smooth projective variety, K_X + mL has enough sections to be "globally generated" once m ≥ n + 1. It was known only in low dimensions. This proves it in every dimension.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Nagata’s conjecture and maximal Seshadri constants
plain_explanation: Nagata's 1959 conjecture says a plane curve of degree d passing through r ≥ 10 general points with multiplicities m_i must satisfy Σ m_i < d·√r. This proves it, together with "maximal Seshadri constants" in higher dimensions.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Bloch’s conjecture for complex surfaces
plain_explanation: Bloch's conjecture says that on a surface with no holomorphic 2-forms (p_g = 0), the group of 0-cycles (formal combinations of points) is as small as possible. This proves it.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Hyperkähler SYZ and projective-space bases
plain_explanation: Hyperkähler manifolds are rigid, highly symmetric spaces that appear in geometry and string theory. This proves the strong SYZ conjecture (certain line bundles produce fibrations) and shows the base of every projective Lagrangian fibration is a projective space.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Oka classification for minimal compact complex surfaces: Kodaira dimension zero and class VII
plain_explanation: Oka manifolds are complex spaces that admit lots of holomorphic maps from ℂⁿ. This proves every K3 surface is Oka, and classifies which minimal surfaces of Kodaira dimension 0 and of class VII are Oka.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: P = W for fixed-determinant SL_n moduli spaces
plain_explanation: "P = W" says two different filtrations on the cohomology of Higgs-bundle moduli spaces, one from topology and one from algebraic geometry, are the same. This proves the fixed-determinant SL_n version in composite rank, which completes all coprime ranks.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: The equivariant cohomological Hikita conjecture
plain_explanation: The Hikita conjecture links the two sides of 3D mirror symmetry: the cohomology of a quiver variety equals the coordinate ring of a fixed locus on the dual "Coulomb branch". This proves the equivariant version for every quiver.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Shafarevich counterexamples in dimension two and with large fundamental group
plain_explanation: Shafarevich conjectured that universal covers of projective varieties are "holomorphically convex". This gives counterexamples: a fourfold with large fundamental group, and a separate surface.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Zariski cancellation and affine fibrations over the complex numbers
plain_explanation: Zariski cancellation asks: if X times a line is ordinary 5-dimensional space, must X be ordinary 4-space? This disproves it over ℂ in dimension 4 by building an "impostor" 4-space that becomes ordinary once one dimension is added. It also disproves the Dolgachev–Weisfeiler fibration conjecture.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: A characteristic-zero counterexample to Lipman–Zariski
plain_explanation: The Lipman–Zariski conjecture says that if a surface's tangent sheaf is free, the surface must be smooth. This gives a counterexample in characteristic zero.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: A stable-coordinate counterexample in four variables
plain_explanation: This builds a polynomial in 4 variables that is not a "coordinate" but becomes one after adding a single extra variable. That disproves the Stable Coordinate and Abhyankar–Sathaye conjectures in this setting.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: A counterexample to Griffiths’ positivity conjecture
plain_explanation: Griffiths conjectured that every ample vector bundle admits a metric with positive (Griffiths) curvature. This gives a counterexample already on the simple surface P¹ × P¹.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Kobayashi’s canonical-ampleness conjecture
plain_explanation: Kobayashi conjectured that compact Kähler manifolds with no entire curves (they are "hyperbolic") must have an ample canonical bundle, which makes them projective. This proves it.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Tangent splittings and product decompositions
plain_explanation: If the tangent bundle of a compact Kähler manifold splits into two well-behaved pieces, this proves the universal cover splits as a product (Beauville's conjecture, two-piece case). It also proves Höring's conjecture for rationally connected manifolds.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: A counterexample to Pixton completeness in Chow
plain_explanation: Pixton conjectured that his relations generate every "tautological" relation on moduli spaces of curves. This gives a counterexample in Chow groups and in cohomology.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Irrational cubic fourfolds with Hodge-theoretic and categorical K3 associations
plain_explanation: Kuznetsov conjectured that a cubic fourfold is rational exactly when it has an associated K3 category. This disproves it: some cubic fourfolds have K3 associations yet are irrational (for large enough discriminant; the threshold is not explicit).

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Gepner symmetry and large-volume stability on threefolds
plain_explanation: Bridgeland stability conditions, an idea that came from string theory, organize the geometry of threefolds. This constructs the special "Gepner point" stability condition on every quintic threefold (Toda's conjecture), and large-volume stability conditions on all Calabi–Yau threefolds.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Termination of projective and Kähler fourfold minimal model programs
plain_explanation: This proves the minimal model program terminates (there is no infinite chain of surgeries called "flips") for projective log canonical fourfolds and Kähler fourfolds. Papers were revised on Oct 7.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Fundamental groups of special complex varieties and root orbifolds
plain_explanation: Campana's abelianity conjecture says that "special" varieties have virtually abelian fundamental groups (their loops commute, up to finite index). This proves it for compact Kähler manifolds, with related results for quasi-projective ones.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Semialgebraic universal covers and bounded domains
plain_explanation: Kollár–Pardon: classify the projective varieties whose universal covers are semialgebraic. They are exactly products of a bounded symmetric domain, ℂ^m and a compact factor. A corollary: a smooth projective variety covered by ℂⁿ is, up to a finite cover, an abelian variety.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Counterexamples to Zariski’s multiplicity conjecture
plain_explanation: Zariski's 1971 multiplicity conjecture says two hypersurface singularities that look identical topologically must have the same multiplicity. This disproves it with explicit counterexamples (multiplicities 2 vs 3, and 4 vs 5 in ℂ⁴).

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: The Global Spherical Shell conjecture
plain_explanation: Class VII surfaces are the last poorly understood family of compact complex surfaces. This proves the Global Spherical Shell conjecture for b₂ > 0, a decisive step toward classifying them completely.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Projective contact classification and the LeBrun–Salamon conjecture
plain_explanation: The LeBrun–Salamon conjecture says positive quaternion-Kähler manifolds must be the standard symmetric "Wolf spaces". This proves it, and classifies projective contact manifolds.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: The generalized Mukai conjecture
plain_explanation: The generalized Mukai conjecture bounds the shape of Fano manifolds: ρ(ι − 1) ≤ n, with equality only for products of projective spaces. This proves it.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Topological triviality of μ-constant surface singularities
plain_explanation: The μ-constant problem: if a family of surface singularities keeps the same Milnor number, is the family topologically trivial? This proves yes for surfaces in ℂ³.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Virasoro constraints for complete intersections and projective-bundle towers
plain_explanation: Virasoro constraints are symmetries that string theory predicts for curve-counting invariants. This proves them for complete intersections in projective space and for towers of projective bundles.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Bounded klt complements for Fano contractions
plain_explanation: This proves Shokurov's bounded-complements conjecture for Fano contractions (finite-coefficient version), a key boundedness tool in classifying shapes.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: The Campana–Peternell conjecture in dimension six
plain_explanation: This proves the Campana–Peternell conjecture in dimension 6: Fano manifolds whose tangent bundle is nef are rational homogeneous spaces.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Anticanonical nonvanishing in every dimension
plain_explanation: If −K_X carries a smooth metric of nonnegative curvature, this proves some power of the anticanonical bundle has a nonzero section, in every dimension.

subject: Algebraic and complex geometry
title: Global quantum geometric Langlands at irrational level
plain_explanation: This proves quantum geometric Langlands at irrational level, in the unramified de Rham setting: an equivalence between categories of twisted D-modules for a group and for its Langlands dual.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Koebe’s circle-domain conjecture
plain_explanation: Koebe's 1908 conjecture: any region of the plane or sphere, however many holes it has, can be reshaped without distorting angles (conformally) into a region whose holes are perfect round disks or points. This proves the existence part, and shows the round-hole picture is rigid when the boundary is "removable" (one direction of the He–Schramm conjecture).

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Brennan's conjecture and the integral-means spectrum
plain_explanation: Brennan's conjecture: for any angle-preserving map from a simply connected region onto the disk, |φ′|^s is area-integrable for 4/3 < s < 4. This proves it with a sharp "integral means" identity, and disproves a prediction of Kraetzer.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: The Falconer distance conjecture
plain_explanation: Falconer's distance conjecture: any set in ℝ^d of fractal dimension greater than d/2 produces a "large" set of distances (positive length). This proves it in every dimension.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Kakeya in three and four dimensions
plain_explanation: The Kakeya problem asks how small a set can be if it contains a unit line segment pointing in every direction. This proves such sets in 4D have full dimension, and proves the stronger "maximal function" version in 3D.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: The L\log L Fourier-convergence conjecture
plain_explanation: When does a function's Fourier series add back up to the function? Carleson proved it happens almost everywhere for square-integrable functions, and Kolmogorov showed it can fail for merely integrable ones. This proves convergence for the in-between class L log L, the conjectured boundary.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Real ultraflat Littlewood polynomials and unbounded binary merit factors
plain_explanation: Littlewood polynomials have every coefficient equal to +1 or −1. Can one be "ultraflat", with the same size (about √N) everywhere on the unit circle? This proves yes, even with real coefficients. As a result, binary ±1 sequences can have arbitrarily low autocorrelation (unbounded "merit factor"), disproving Turyn's conjecture.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Fourier restriction for positively curved surfaces
plain_explanation: Fourier restriction asks how well the Fourier transform of something living on a curved surface spreads into space. This proves the conjectured bound (p > 3) for every positively curved surface in 3D, including the sphere: the famous restriction conjecture in three dimensions.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: The three-dimensional Bochner–Riesz conjecture
plain_explanation: Bochner–Riesz means smooth out a sharp Fourier cut-off to a ball. The conjecture predicts exactly which smoothing orders keep the operator bounded on L^p. This resolves it in 3D.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Local smoothing in three dimensions
plain_explanation: Sogge's local smoothing conjecture says waves become smoother when you average over a short time window rather than look at a single moment. This proves it in 3D over the full range of exponents.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: The exact Sobolev endpoint for Schrödinger convergence
plain_explanation: Carleson's problem: if you start the free Schrödinger equation from data f, does the solution return to f point by point as time goes to 0? This was known to need f in H^s with s ≥ n/(2(n+1)). This proves convergence exactly at that endpoint.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Riesz transforms and rectifiability in higher codimension
plain_explanation: If a measure's Riesz transform is bounded, must the measure be made of smooth pieces ("rectifiable")? This resolves the remaining higher-codimension cases.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Annular variation and dyadic absolute bounds for the triangular Hilbert transform
plain_explanation: The triangular Hilbert transform is a notoriously hard multilinear singular integral. This proves bounds for it at the symmetric L³ point, with variation and maximal versions.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Hilbert transforms along Lipschitz directions
plain_explanation: This gives a uniform L² bound for the Hilbert transform taken along a Lipschitz field of directions at short scales, establishing Stein's weak-type conjecture in that regime.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: The geometric case of the Erdős similarity conjecture
plain_explanation: Erdős's similarity conjecture says that for every infinite set of numbers, some set of positive measure contains no shifted, rescaled copy of it. This proves it for every geometric progression {qⁿ}.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: Endpoint Sobolev regularity of centered disk averages
plain_explanation: Averaging a function over disks and taking the largest average (the maximal function) does not increase its total variation (W^{1,1} norm) in 2D. This resolves the centered-disk case of the Hajłasz–Onninen problem.

subject: Real and complex analysis
title: An L^3 bound for the trilinear Hilbert transform
plain_explanation: The trilinear Hilbert transform with shifts t, 2t, 3t is shown to be bounded from L³ × L³ × L³ to L¹, a long-sought case.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: The Mahler conjectures, functional inequalities and polar-product symplectic width
plain_explanation: Mahler's conjecture: for a convex body K and its "polar" dual K°, the product vol(K)·vol(K°) is smallest for the cube (symmetric case) and the simplex (general case). This proves both in every dimension, with all equality cases, and computes a related symplectic width. It is one of the best-known problems in convex geometry.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Sharp projection-body inequalities and a counterexample to simplex maximization
plain_explanation: A projection body records the shadow areas of a convex body in every direction. Petty's conjecture (ellipsoids minimize projection-body volume at fixed volume) is proven for n ≥ 4, completing it. It also shows simplices are not the maximizers, because products of simplices beat them.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Bounded-distortion L_1 embeddings of planar and bounded-treewidth graphs
plain_explanation: Can shortest-path distances in a planar network be represented faithfully as L1 ("Manhattan-style") distances? This proves yes, with bounded distortion, for planar graphs and for graphs of bounded treewidth. Consequence: in such networks, the maximum multi-route flow and the minimum cut differ by at most a constant factor.
politeia_note: Road and transit networks are nearly planar. This guarantees that cut-based bottleneck analysis ("which few links, if closed, split the city?") is within a constant factor of true multi-route capacity. It is background for any capacity or bottleneck layer on a map; existing tools already compute this.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Triangular-lattice optimality, long-range Riesz and Coulomb energies, and spherical logarithmic energy
plain_explanation: Among all ways to spread points in the plane at a given density, the triangular (honeycomb) lattice minimizes energy for a very wide class of repulsive interactions ("universal optimality" in 2D). This also settles the Coulomb and Riesz versions (Sandier–Serfaty) and logarithmic energy on the sphere.
politeia_note: Hexagonal arrangements are provably the most even way to spread points over a plane for any repulsive cost. That backs using hexagon bins for map aggregation and evenly spaced placement (sensors, kiosks, sample points). This is already common practice; the result is the strongest theoretical support for it.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Logarithmic and L_p Brunn–Minkowski inequalities and the B-conjecture
plain_explanation: The log Brunn–Minkowski inequality is a strengthened "volume of a blend" inequality for symmetric convex bodies. This proves it in every dimension, along with the B-conjecture for even log-concave measures.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: The optimal order of convex-body covering density
plain_explanation: How efficiently can you cover space with translated copies of one convex shape? This proves the worst-case covering density is on the order of n·log n in dimension n, and that lattice coverings achieve it.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Dimension-free logarithmic Sobolev inequality for subgaussian log-concave measures
plain_explanation: Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities control how tightly random quantities concentrate around their averages. This proves a version whose constant does not grow with dimension for log-concave distributions whose one-dimensional views are sub-Gaussian.
quant_note: Background for risk modelling: for well-behaved (log-concave, sub-Gaussian) distributions, concentration bounds do not get worse as you add assets. Real returns are fat-tailed, so it mostly tells you which assumptions buy clean concentration.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Subpolynomial dimension reduction in L_p
plain_explanation: Dimension reduction: can n points be squeezed into few dimensions while keeping all distances within a factor D? For ordinary Euclidean distance about log n dimensions suffice (Johnson–Lindenstrauss). For other L_p distances it was unclear. This shows n^{o(1)} dimensions suffice for every 1 < p < ∞.
quant_note: Background for compressing large feature sets for "find past days like today" searches under non-Euclidean distances. How practical the construction is remains unclear; random projections are still the tool for ordinary distance.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Hyperbolicity cones without semidefinite lifts
plain_explanation: Hyperbolicity cones are convex shapes that come from optimization. The generalized Lax conjecture said they can all be written as slices of semidefinite cones, which would make them solvable by standard SDP software. This disproves it: some of them cannot be written that way at all.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: The Gaussian propeller conjecture in every dimension
plain_explanation: Split space into pieces and measure each piece's Gaussian "centre of mass". The sum of their squares is at most 9/(8π), achieved by three 120° wedges (the "propeller"). One consequence is a hardness result for approximate kernel clustering.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: The Euclidean Steinitz–Bergström bound
plain_explanation: Take any sequence of arrows (vectors) of length at most 1 in d dimensions. You can pick a + or − for each one, in order, so that every running total stays within C·√d, however long the sequence is. Equivalently, any set of arrows that sums to zero can be put in an order whose running totals all stay within C·√d. The √d size is optimal.
quant_note: This is about ordering trades so temporary exposure stays small. A rebalance is a set of trades whose net factor exposures sum to about zero. The theorem says some execution order always keeps the running exposure in every factor within C·√d × (largest single trade), however many trades there are. To test: on real rebalances, compare naive order against a greedy balancing order (each step, execute the trade that keeps running exposure smallest), and measure peak intermediate exposure and slippage. The paper proves such an order exists; the greedy heuristic is what you would actually run.
politeia_note: For sequential fairness: when approving items one at a time (projects, budget lines) that affect d groups or districts, some order (or choice of which side to fund) keeps every group's running balance within C·√d. Useful framing for a "keep it balanced as we go" allocation view.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Compact counterexamples to bi-Lipschitz dimension reduction
plain_explanation: Sets that look finite-dimensional at every scale ("doubling" sets) still need not fit into any finite-dimensional space without distortion, even compact pieces of Hilbert space. This answers the Lang–Plaut problem negatively.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: The sharp exponential scale of edit-distance distortion
plain_explanation: Edit distance (the fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one string into another) cannot be represented faithfully as an L1 distance. This finds the best possible distortion exactly: exp(Θ(√(log d · log log d))).
quant_note: If you encode bars or regimes as symbol strings and compare sequences by edit distance, you cannot turn that into a fast vector (L1) similarity without real distortion. Keep edit distance as a separate re-ranking step on a short list of candidates.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: Cylinder coverings below the half-area bound
plain_explanation: This covers a regular tetrahedron with finitely many cylinders whose total cross-section area is less than half its smallest shadow, disproving Bang-type "half-area" covering bounds in 3D.

subject: Convex and metric geometry
title: The sharp simplex conjecture for isotropic constants
plain_explanation: Among all convex bodies, the simplex has the most "lopsided" spread of volume (the largest isotropic constant), resolving the strong isotropic constant conjecture. This also proves a sharp lower bound on the entropy of log-concave densities.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: The Unique Games Conjecture and optimal approximation thresholds
plain_explanation: The Unique Games Conjecture (Khot, 2002) is the central open problem about approximation algorithms, and this proves it. As a consequence, many simple approximation algorithms are the best possible unless P = NP. For example, Goemans–Williamson's 0.878 for Max-Cut and factor 2 for Vertex Cover cannot be beaten. The family also gives direct proofs of these consequences.
quant_note: Splitting assets into two books so the most anti-correlated pairs land on opposite sides is a Max-Cut problem. The Goemans–Williamson semidefinite rounding is now proven to be the best possible general guarantee (unless P = NP). For a few hundred assets use that method or an exact solver; don't expect a cleverer general algorithm.
politeia_note: Splitting a disagreement network (who votes against whom) into two camps is also Max-Cut. If Politeia ever shows a "polarization split", the same method is provably the best general approach, and exact solvers are fine for small groups.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Exact derandomization of logarithmic space: L=RL=BPL
plain_explanation: L = BPL: anything a computer can solve with randomness and very little memory (logarithmic space) can be solved with the same memory and no randomness at all. A landmark in derandomization.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Quasipolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff, stochastic and parity games
plain_explanation: In mean-payoff games, two players push a token around a graph collecting rewards, and the question is who can guarantee a positive long-run average. Whether this can be solved in polynomial time is a famous open question. This gives quasipolynomial algorithms (2^{O(log² L)} steps) for plain, stochastic, and parity versions, including optimal stationary strategies.
quant_note: Background: finite long-run-average games are how you would formally model, say, a liquidity provider against adversarial flow. These results say exact optimal stationary strategies are computable in near-polynomial time for finite models. Real markets are not finite turn-based games, so this is framing, not a tool.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Perfect completeness for 2-to-1 games
plain_explanation: This proves Khot's 2-to-1 Games Conjecture with perfect completeness: it is NP-hard to tell fully satisfiable instances of these constraint games from ones where almost nothing can be satisfied.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Hardness of coloring three-colorable graphs
plain_explanation: Even when a graph is known to be colourable with 3 colours, finding a colouring with any fixed number of colours (say 1,000) is NP-hard. This settles a classic hardness question.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Matrix multiplication with exponent at most 9/4
plain_explanation: The matrix multiplication exponent ω is pushed from about 2.371 down to at most 9/4 = 2.25 over ℂ. In theory, n×n matrices can be multiplied in about n^2.25 steps. These are "galactic" algorithms with astronomically large hidden constants.
quant_note: Covariance, regression and PCA will not get faster from this at real sizes.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: A cubic permanent–determinant lower bound
plain_explanation: The permanent-versus-determinant problem is the algebraic version of P vs NP. This proves that writing the n×n permanent as a determinant, even approximately, needs a matrix of size at least c·n³, the first cubic lower bound.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Integer multiplication below n\log n
plain_explanation: This multiplies two n-bit integers in slightly less than n·log n time, disproving the Schönhage–Strassen optimality conjecture in the multitape Turing machine model. The saving factor (log n)^κ with κ = 2^−182 is purely theoretical.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Optimal-order randomized k-server on arbitrary metrics
plain_explanation: In the k-server problem, k servers (think repair trucks) must move to serve requests that arrive one at a time at points of a space, keeping total travel close to the best plan made in hindsight. This proves randomized strategies within O(log² k) of hindsight exist on every space, the optimal order. The extra additive travel cost can be enormous.
quant_note: Repositioning k resting orders (a ladder or grid) as price moves around is a k-server-like problem. The result says the right benchmark is about log² k times the hindsight-optimal movement. This is framing only; the algorithm is not practical.
politeia_note: Dispatching k mobile units (inspectors, repair crews, mobile service vans) to requests that appear over time is literally k-server. Background for any live dispatch view; real dispatch uses simple heuristics such as nearest-available plus rebalancing.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: One-sample matroid prophet inequalities against an almighty adversary
plain_explanation: In a prophet inequality, values arrive one at a time and you must accept or reject each on the spot, subject to limits on what combination you may keep (a "matroid": for example at most k items, or at most one per category). This shows that seeing just one past sample per item is enough to guarantee a constant fraction of the hindsight optimum, even against an adversary who knows everything. The constant is 2^−310, so it proves possibility rather than giving a usable guarantee.
quant_note: This is the setup when you can hold only k positions (or one per sector or instrument) and must decide on each signal as it arrives. Practical version: set each slot's acceptance threshold from one past sample, such as last period's best signal strength for that slot. For a single slot, "take the first signal that beats the best past sample" already has a known 1/2 guarantee. To test on your signal log: compare threshold-from-last-period against fixed thresholds, measured as captured edge versus hindsight-best selection.
politeia_note: Proposals or volunteer offers that arrive over time, with caps (budget slots, one per district) and on-the-spot decisions: set thresholds from last cycle's data. Framing for "rolling approval" flows.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Beyond the square-root exponent for depth-three circuits
plain_explanation: This gives an explicit function that needs more than 2^{ω(√n)} gates in depth-3 OR–AND–OR circuits, breaking a long-standing barrier for circuit lower bounds.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Approximate counting and entropy of perfect matchings
plain_explanation: Counting perfect matchings (ways to pair up all vertices of a graph) exactly is #P-hard. This gives the first efficient randomized approximate counter (an FPRAS) for every graph, a decades-old open problem, plus a sharp entropy bound.
politeia_note: Fair random pairing (citizens for deliberation pairs, mentors, reviewers) when only some pairings are allowed. Efficient approximate counting implies near-uniform random sampling of valid pairings, so every allowed pairing is almost equally likely, a fairness promise you can state publicly. A practical version would need engineering.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Approximate counting of common integer polymatroid bases
plain_explanation: This gives an efficient randomized approximate counter for the common "bases" of two matroids or polymatroids (for example, structures that are valid in two systems at once).

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Sampling and counting contingency tables with arbitrary margins
plain_explanation: A contingency table here is a grid of non-negative whole numbers with fixed row totals and fixed column totals. This gives an exact uniformly random sampler, and an efficient approximate counter, for any sizes and any totals.
quant_note: Fixed-total tables are the null model for "is this co-occurrence real?" Example: rows are your patterns or signals, columns are market regimes (or sessions or weekdays), and cells count hits. Sample random tables with the same row and column totals to get an exact p-value for "pattern X clusters in regime Y" that accounts for how often each pattern fires and how common each regime is. In practice use existing samplers (sequential importance sampling or MCMC); the new result guarantees exact uniform sampling is efficient for any totals.
politeia_note: Two strong uses. (1) Privacy: release synthetic tables (say, service use by district × age band) that match the published totals exactly without exposing real records. (2) Audits: test whether a district × option table of votes or usage is surprising given its totals.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Uniform black-box noncommutative identity testing across characteristics
plain_explanation: This gives deterministic black-box tests for whether a noncommutative formula is secretly zero, uniformly across all field characteristics.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Uniform sparsest cut: hardness and semidefinite gaps
plain_explanation: Sparsest cut asks for the weakest bottleneck that splits a network into two parts, relative to their sizes. This proves even constant-factor approximation is NP-hard, and that the standard semidefinite relaxation can be off by about √(log n).
quant_note: Clustering assets by cutting a correlation network at its weakest bottleneck is a sparsest-cut problem. There is no constant-factor guarantee in general, so treat spectral or semidefinite cluster splits as heuristics and check them with stability tests.
politeia_note: The same goes for community maps: "where does this community split?" has no guaranteed near-optimal answer. Show such splits as suggestions, not facts.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Bin packing and unbounded configuration-LP gaps
plain_explanation: Bin packing means fitting items into as few bins as possible. This shows the popular linear-programming lower bound can be off by any fixed additive amount, and that approximating within a fixed additive amount is NP-hard.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: The Courtade–Kumar and Hellinger conjectures
plain_explanation: If you compress n random bits into a single yes/no bit, which compression keeps the most information about a noisy copy of the input? Courtade and Kumar conjectured the answer is to just copy one bit (a "dictator"). This proves it, along with the related Hellinger conjecture.
quant_note: A counter-intuitive point for signal aggregation: when you squash many noisy binary indicators into one bit, a majority-style vote does not keep more information about the inputs than reading the single best input. If your one-bit "consensus" signal does not beat its best component out of sample, this is part of why. (It concerns information about the inputs, not directly about future returns.)
politeia_note: This connects to a classic tension in voting theory: majority vote is the most stable summary under noise, yet the summary carrying the most information about individual inputs is the "dictator". Good material for a civic explainer on why one-number summaries of public opinion lose information, and why to show the full distribution.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Almost-linear-time exact matching and prescribed-degree factors in general graphs
plain_explanation: Maximum matching (pairing up as many vertices as possible) in any graph is solved in almost-linear time, a landmark speed-up over the classic m·√n bound.
politeia_note: Fast exact matching at city scale (volunteers to tasks, residents to appointment slots) when compatibility is yes or no. Existing algorithms already handle realistic sizes; this mostly removes worst-case worries.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Almost-linear approximation of edit distance
plain_explanation: Edit distance (the fewest single-character edits that turn one string into another) is approximated within 1 + ε in almost-linear time. Exact edit distance is believed to need about quadratic time, so this is close to the best possible.
quant_note: If you turn sessions into symbol strings (for example a 64-state regime code), edit distance finds historical analogues that match up to shifts and insertions. This says approximate edit distance can scale to very long histories in principle. At normal data sizes, ordinary dynamic programming is fine.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Quantitative trace-reconstruction bounds with a uniform decoder
plain_explanation: Trace reconstruction: recover a hidden binary string from many copies, each with random deletions. This proves n^{Ω(log log n)} copies are needed (so no polynomial number suffices), and gives quasipolynomial algorithms.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Polynomial-time scheduling on three identical machines
plain_explanation: Scheduling unit-length jobs with "this before that" constraints on 3 identical machines to finish as early as possible has been open since Garey and Johnson (1979). This solves it in polynomial time.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: The metric k-median approximation threshold and recovery
plain_explanation: In k-median you open k facilities among candidate sites so that the total distance from every client to its nearest open facility is as small as possible. This gives a (1 + 2/e + ε) ≈ 1.736 approximation, and shows that is the best possible unless P = NP.
quant_note: k-medoids clustering of market days (pick k representative days) is the same problem. Useful for choosing "representative regimes" for scenario tests.
politeia_note: This is the "where should the next k clinics, libraries or polling stations go?" question on a map. The result fixes the gold-standard guarantee (about 1.74× optimal). In practice, use local-search or integer-programming solvers at city scale, and show citizens the total travel distance each option implies: a simple, honest comparison view.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Exponential semidefinite complexity of perfect matching
plain_explanation: This proves every exact semidefinite description of the perfect-matching polytope must be exponentially large, answering Rothvoss's question negatively.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Average sensitivity of polynomial threshold functions
plain_explanation: A polynomial threshold function decides yes or no from the sign of a degree-d polynomial in n inputs that are each ±1; a weighted vote is the degree-1 case. This proves that, on average, at most 8d·√n of the n inputs are "pivotal" (flipping that one input changes the outcome). This is the Gotsman–Linial conjecture.
quant_note: A linear trading rule over n binary features is a degree-1 threshold function. The bound limits how often single-feature flips change the decision overall, a robustness lens for rule-based systems.
politeia_note: For any weighted-vote rule over n voters, the expected number of pivotal voters is at most 8√n. So an individual's chance of being decisive in a large vote is typically about 1/√n or less. A crisp, honest fact for civic-education screens.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: A factor-two approximation for shortest common superstring
plain_explanation: The shortest common superstring problem asks for the shortest string containing every given string. This gives a long-conjectured factor-2 approximation in polynomial time.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Exponential state costs for two-way automata
plain_explanation: This proves exponential lower bounds on the number of states two-way finite automata need for certain tasks, resolving the Sakoda–Sipser conjecture over growing alphabets.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Exact Fourier transforms below n\log n
plain_explanation: This computes the exact discrete Fourier transform in fewer than n·log n operations. The saving factor is (log n)^(10^−13), so it is purely theoretical.
quant_note: FFT-based filters and spectral analysis will not get faster from this.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Rapid mixing of graph switches for every degree sequence
plain_explanation: Random networks with a prescribed degree sequence (everyone keeps their number of links) can be generated by repeatedly swapping pairs of edges. This proves the swapping process mixes in polynomial time for every degree sequence (the Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture), and gives an exact uniform sampler.
quant_note: This is the standard null model for networks. Are the clusters in your correlation or lead–lag network real, or a side-effect of some assets having many links? Rewire edges while keeping each node's degree, then compare. This result guarantees that rewiring approach is sound for any degree pattern.
politeia_note: Use the same check for civic networks (who co-signs whose proposals): before showing "communities" or "influencers", compare against degree-preserving random rewiring.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: A superquadratic separation of sensitivity and block sensitivity
plain_explanation: This builds Boolean functions whose block sensitivity grows faster than the square of their sensitivity, disproving the quadratic strengthening of the Sensitivity Conjecture.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: The computational complexity of Weisfeiler–Leman refinement
plain_explanation: Weisfeiler–Leman refinement underlies graph-isomorphism heuristics and limits what graph neural networks can tell apart. This proves unconditional n^{Ω(k)} time lower bounds for it, and EXPTIME-completeness when k is part of the input.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Generalized star height at most three
plain_explanation: Every regular language can be written as a generalized regular expression (with complement allowed) using at most three nested Kleene stars, an absolute bound.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Homogeneous depth-five lower bounds for iterated matrix multiplication
plain_explanation: The (1,1) entry of a product of n matrices of variables needs n^{Θ(√n)} gates in homogeneous depth-5 arithmetic circuits, a sharp lower bound.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: A quasilinear PCP theorem for PPAD
plain_explanation: This proves a quasilinear-size PCP theorem for PPAD, the complexity class behind finding Nash equilibria and fixed points: approximate solutions can be checked robustly and locally.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: One-tape time simulation in two-fifths-power space
plain_explanation: Any time-T computation of a one-tape machine can be simulated in about T^{2/5} memory, improving the previous square-root bound.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Subset Sum in O(2^{0.49n}) time
plain_explanation: Subset Sum (choose numbers from a list that add up to a target) is solved in 2^{0.49n} time in the worst case. This is the first improvement on the 2^{n/2} "meet in the middle" barrier from 1974.
politeia_note: Choosing projects whose costs add up exactly to a budget is a Subset Sum problem. Worst-case cost drops to 2^{0.49n}, which is still exponential. At realistic participatory-budget sizes, standard knapsack or integer-programming solvers are what you use.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Subpolynomial query complexity for log-concave sampling
plain_explanation: Sampling from log-concave distributions (well-behaved bell-like shapes) using gradient queries: the number of queries can grow more slowly than any power of the dimension, so the optimal exponent is zero.
quant_note: For Bayesian parameter uncertainty in strategy models (posterior sampling with Langevin or HMC-type methods), in the well-conditioned case dimension is not the bottleneck. Real posteriors are often badly conditioned, so practical gains need preconditioning.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Memory–sample lower bounds for noiseless Gaussian regression
plain_explanation: A one-pass learner with limited memory (about d² bits) needs on the order of d·log(1/ε) exact Gaussian measurements to recover an unknown direction to accuracy ε.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Existential–universal real sentences in the counting hierarchy
plain_explanation: Deciding the truth of sentences about real numbers with one ∃∀ quantifier alternation lies in the counting hierarchy, a strong new upper bound for the existential theory of the reals.

subject: Theoretical computer science
title: Deterministic polynomial factorization over prime fields
plain_explanation: This factors any polynomial over a prime field 𝔽_p deterministically in polynomial time, with no randomness and no Riemann-hypothesis assumption. It is a long-standing open problem; randomized algorithms have existed for decades.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Hilbert's sixteenth problem: uniform bounds for limit cycles
plain_explanation: The second half of Hilbert's 16th problem (1900) asks how many isolated cycles ("limit cycles") a planar polynomial vector field of degree n can have. This proves there is a finite maximum that depends only on n, one of the most famous open questions in dynamics. It also shows classical quintic Liénard systems have at most two.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Banach’s simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem
plain_explanation: Banach's simple Lebesgue spectrum problem: this builds a smooth, volume-preserving map of the 3-torus in which the past and future iterates of a single observable form a perfect orthonormal basis, so the dynamics is completely "spread out" yet built from one signal.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Rokhlin’s multiple-mixing problem
plain_explanation: A system is "mixing" if any two events become independent as the time gap between them grows. Rokhlin asked in 1949 whether that automatically makes any finite number of events jointly independent when all their gaps grow ("mixing of all orders"). This proves yes, for a single transformation.
quant_note: In stationary-process terms: if any two events become independent as their time gap grows, then all higher-order dependencies fade too. It supports checking pairwise decay in stationary models, but markets are not stationary, so treat it as background.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Positive metric entropy for the standard map
plain_explanation: The standard (Chirikov) map is a textbook model of chaos. This proves it has genuine chaos on a set of positive area (positive metric entropy) for every large enough parameter, Sinai's conjecture.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: The near-boundary Birkhoff conjecture
plain_explanation: The Birkhoff conjecture says the only convex billiard tables whose trajectories near the edge are organized into smooth invariant curves are ellipses. This proves the near-boundary version.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: The entropy-rate dimension formula for self-similar measures
plain_explanation: Self-similar measures are fractals made by repeatedly shrinking copies of themselves. This proves their dimension equals min(1, entropy rate ÷ average contraction), even when the copies overlap.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Classwise permanence for weakly reversible mass-action systems
plain_explanation: For chemical reaction networks with mass-action kinetics (weakly reversible ones), this proves "permanence": every species' concentration eventually stays between fixed positive lower and finite upper bounds, so nothing dies out or blows up.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Weak mixing of triangular billiards with an irrational angle
plain_explanation: For a billiard ball in any triangle with at least one angle that is an irrational multiple of π, this proves the motion is weakly mixing: the ball eventually "forgets" where it started, in a statistical sense.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: A C^1 counterexample to the entropy conjecture
plain_explanation: Shub's entropy conjecture says that maps which stretch topology (homology) a lot must be chaotic (positive topological entropy). This disproves it for C¹ maps.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Zero entropy does not guarantee a smooth positive-volume model
plain_explanation: This builds a zero-entropy (non-chaotic) system that cannot be realized as any smooth volume-preserving system on any manifold.

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Arithmetic classification and non-Pisot singularity for Bernoulli convolutions
plain_explanation: Bernoulli convolutions are the distributions of random series Σ ±λⁿ with fair coin-flip signs. This classifies exactly when the result is smooth and when it is singular, and finds new singular cases (reciprocals of quartic Salem numbers).

subject: Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
title: Pointwise multiple ergodic averages for mixing transformations
plain_explanation: This proves that multiple ergodic averages (time averages of products like f(Tⁿx)·g(T²ⁿx)·…) converge at almost every point for mixing transformations, with the expected limit.
quant_note: See 145 for the related time-series intuition.

subject: Combinatorics
title: A counterexample to periodic tiling in dimension three
plain_explanation: Periodic tiling conjecture: if one shape tiles space by sliding copies around, can it also tile in a repeating (periodic) pattern? This gives a counterexample in 3D, the smallest dimension where one can exist.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Borsuk's conjecture fails in dimension nine
plain_explanation: Borsuk's conjecture says every bounded set in ℝ^d can be split into d + 1 pieces of smaller diameter. It was known to fail in dimension 64 and up; this shows it already fails in dimension 9.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Graph coloring, clique minors, and Colin de Verdière invariants
plain_explanation: Hadwiger's conjecture (1943), one of the most famous in graph theory, says any graph that needs k colours contains the complete graph K_k as a "minor". This disproves it, even in a fractional form. On the positive side, the list-colouring number is at most a constant times the Hadwiger number.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The Euclidean plane cannot be colored with five colors
plain_explanation: Hadwiger–Nelson problem: how many colours are needed to paint the plane so that no two points exactly 1 apart share a colour? Known: between 5 and 7. This proves 5 colours are not enough, leaving only 6 or 7.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Erdős’s reciprocal-sum conjecture and quasipolynomial Szemerédi bounds
plain_explanation: Erdős's famous conjecture (a $5,000 Erdős problem): if a set of positive integers has Σ 1/n = ∞, as the primes do, it contains arithmetic progressions of every length. This proves it, with much better (quasipolynomial) bounds in Szemerédi's theorem.
quant_note: The Ramsey-theory lesson (also 160, 164, 170, 171): any large enough set or colouring must contain regular patterns. Finding a pattern in a large dataset is therefore guaranteed by size alone and is not evidence of an edge. Validate every catalogued pattern out of sample, with multiple-testing corrections.
politeia_note: The same caution applies to civic dashboards: "striking" patterns in large datasets can be inevitable. Add a "could this be chance?" check before highlighting one.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Superexponential van der Waerden numbers
plain_explanation: The van der Waerden number W_r(k) is the shortest run of integers that forces a single-coloured k-term arithmetic progression in any r-colouring. This proves it grows faster than exponentially, answering Erdős.
quant_note: See 159.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Counterexamples to Sidorenko’s conjecture and the forcing conjecture
plain_explanation: Sidorenko's conjecture says a random graph contains the fewest copies of any bipartite pattern for its edge density. This disproves it with a 35-vertex counterexample, and also disproves the related "forcing" conjecture.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Counterexamples to Ryser’s covering conjecture
plain_explanation: Ryser's conjecture bounds how many vertices are needed to touch every edge of certain hypergraphs. This disproves it for infinitely many sizes, and also disproves Gyárfás's tree-cover conjecture.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Hindman’s finite sums and products conjecture
plain_explanation: Hindman's conjecture: however you colour the positive integers with finitely many colours, there are arbitrarily large finite sets whose subset sums and subset products all have the same colour. This proves it.
quant_note: See 159.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The Harary–Hill and Zarankiewicz crossing-number formulas
plain_explanation: What is the fewest number of crossings when you draw the complete graph K_n (every pair connected) in the plane? Harary and Hill gave a formula, and Zarankiewicz did the same for K_{m,n} (Turán's brickyard problem). This proves both formulas: the classical drawings are optimal.
politeia_note: For network diagrams: a dense "everyone linked to everyone" view has unavoidable crossings, at a now-known minimum. For dense relationship data use matrix (heat-map) or edge-bundled layouts instead of node-link drawings.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The higher-dimensional Erdős distinct-distances conjecture
plain_explanation: Erdős's distinct-distances problem in higher dimensions: any n points in ℝ^d determine at least c·n^{2/d} different distances, which matches the grid. Proven for every fixed d ≥ 3.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Planar distinct distances and unit-distance bounds
plain_explanation: In the plane, this proves almost every point of an n-point set sees nearly n different distances (the weak pinned version), and improves the unit-distance bound to O(n^{4/3−δ}), the first progress since 1984.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials
plain_explanation: Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials are central objects in representation theory. The combinatorial invariance conjecture (1980s) says they depend only on the shape of a certain ordered interval. This proves it in full generality.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Shareshian–Wachs elementary positivity
plain_explanation: This proves the Shareshian–Wachs refinement of the Stanley–Stembridge conjecture: chromatic quasisymmetric functions of unit interval graphs expand positively in the elementary basis, with an explicit counting rule.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Sharp logarithmic exponents for off-diagonal Ramsey numbers
plain_explanation: The off-diagonal Ramsey number r(s, t) is the smallest group size that forces s mutual friends or t mutual strangers. For each fixed s ≥ 5, this pins down its growth in t, including the logarithmic factor.
quant_note: See 159.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The hypercube Ramsey conjecture
plain_explanation: The Burr–Erdős hypercube conjecture: the Ramsey number of the n-dimensional cube graph is only a constant times its number of vertices (2ⁿ). Proven.
quant_note: See 159.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Classification of finite Euclidean Ramsey configurations
plain_explanation: This classifies exactly which finite point patterns are "Euclidean Ramsey", meaning they appear in a single colour in every finite colouring of high-dimensional space, and disproves the Leader–Russell–Walters conjecture.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
plain_explanation: Seymour's second-neighbourhood conjecture: in any directed network with no two-way links, some vertex reaches at least as many vertices in exactly two steps as in one step. This proves it.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Deterministic construction of strong thin spanning trees
plain_explanation: The strong thin-tree conjecture: every k-edge-connected graph has a spanning tree that uses only about a C/k fraction of the edges of every cut. This proves it, with a polynomial-time construction. Thin trees are a key tool for travelling-salesman approximation.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Talagrand’s expectation thresholds, discrete convexity, and graph decompositions
plain_explanation: For random structures, this proves the "integral" and "fractional" expectation thresholds agree up to a constant (a Talagrand conjecture), resolves Talagrand's discrete-convexity conjecture, and proves a graph-decomposition conjecture.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The second Kahn–Kalai conjecture with an edge-count bound
plain_explanation: The second Kahn–Kalai conjecture: the edge density at which a random graph contains a copy of H is at most a log factor above an easy expectation bound. This proves it.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Bounded-degree coboundary expanders
plain_explanation: This builds bounded-degree "coboundary expanders" (high-dimensional cousins of expander graphs) in every dimension. These matter for quantum error-correcting codes and property testing.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Deterministic nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs in every fixed degree
plain_explanation: Ramanujan graphs are the best possible expanders: sparse networks with the fastest possible mixing and no bottlenecks. This constructs them deterministically, for every degree d ≥ 3 and every large even size, in a non-bipartite form.
politeia_note: If Politeia ever links local groups or delegates in a sparse network (who passes information to whom), Ramanujan graphs are the gold standard: few links, fast spread, no bottlenecks. A deterministic construction means the network design is reproducible and auditable.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The circulant Hadamard and Barker-sequence conjectures
plain_explanation: Ryser's circulant Hadamard conjecture: a circulant ±1 matrix with orthogonal rows exists only in sizes 1 and 4. Proven. As a result, "Barker sequences" (binary codes with tiny autocorrelation, used in radar) exist only at the known lengths 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 11, 13.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Barnette’s Hamiltonian-cycle conjecture
plain_explanation: Barnette's conjecture: every cubic, bipartite, planar, 3-connected graph has a Hamiltonian cycle (a tour visiting every vertex exactly once). Proven.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The Erdős–Gallai cycle-decomposition conjecture
plain_explanation: The Erdős–Gallai conjecture: the edges of any n-vertex graph can be split into at most C·n cycles and single edges. Proven.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Power savings for intersective polynomial differences and prime arguments
plain_explanation: Sets of integers that avoid having two members differ by a polynomial value (for example a perfect square) must be small. This proves power-saving bounds, including when the polynomial is evaluated at primes.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Power savings for planar halving lines and k-sets
plain_explanation: Halving lines split a planar point set into two equal halves. This proves there are at most O(n^{4/3−ε}) of them (for points with no three on a line), the first improvement in decades.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Correspondence coloring with a fixed forbidden subgraph
plain_explanation: Graphs that avoid any fixed subgraph can be coloured with about Δ/log Δ colours (Alon–Krivelevich–Sudakov), and K_r-free graphs have large independent sets (Ajtai–Erdős–Komlós–Szemerédi). Both are proven.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Counterexamples to infinite matroid intersection and packing/covering
plain_explanation: The infinite matroid intersection and packing/covering conjectures are disproved, using two self-dual matroids on a countable set.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Uniform influence and sharp thresholds for graph and hypergraph properties
plain_explanation: Friedgut–Kalai: every symmetric property of random graphs that only gets more likely as edges are added switches from "unlikely" to "almost certain" within a window of width O(1/log² n) of the edge probability, a sharp threshold. Proven, with hypergraph versions.
politeia_note: When a feature only works once enough participants connect (for example, a discussion network becoming fully connected), expect a tipping point: the switch from rare to near-certain happens over a narrow range. Plan rollouts and dashboards for thresholds, not steady linear growth.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Snaky in 21 Maker moves
plain_explanation: In a Maker–Breaker game on an infinite grid (a tic-tac-toe relative), Maker can force the 6-cell "Snaky" shape within 21 of their own moves. This settles the last open case of Harary's achievement games.

subject: Combinatorics
title: The sharp terminal leave in random triangle removal
plain_explanation: Start from a complete graph and repeatedly delete a random triangle until none is left. About n^{3/2}/(2√2) edges remain at the end, as conjectured.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Cycle–clique Ramsey numbers
plain_explanation: This proves the exact Ramsey number for cycles versus cliques: R(C_m, K_n) = (m − 1)(n − 1) + 1 for all m ≥ n ≥ 3, except R(C_3, K_3) = 6.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Polynomial removal fails for ordered binary matrices
plain_explanation: The "removal lemma" for ordered binary matrices cannot have polynomial bounds: this gives one fixed 66 × 66 pattern that defeats every proposed polynomial bound.

subject: Combinatorics
title: A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound
plain_explanation: Heilbronn's triangle problem: place n points in a square so the smallest triangle they form is as large as possible. This shows you can beat n^{−2} by a power, disproving the conjectured upper bound.

subject: Combinatorics
title: Boolean functions violate the square-root degree bound by arbitrary factors
plain_explanation: For Boolean functions, the total correlation with single input bits can exceed C·√(degree) for any constant C, disproving a proposed bound.

subject: Algebra
title: Serre’s intersection-multiplicity conjecture
plain_explanation: Serre's intersection-multiplicity conjecture (positivity) is proven in the last open case, ramified mixed characteristic. Intersection multiplicities are how algebra counts how many times shapes meet.

subject: Algebra
title: Lech’s multiplicity conjecture
plain_explanation: Lech's conjecture (1960): multiplicity, a measure of how singular a point is, cannot go down along flat maps of local rings. Proven in every dimension and characteristic.

subject: Algebra
title: A counterexample to the small Cohen–Macaulay module conjecture
plain_explanation: The small Cohen–Macaulay module conjecture is disproved: this gives a three-dimensional complete local domain over ℂ with no nonzero finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module.

subject: Algebra
title: A counterexample to Kaplansky’s zero-divisor conjecture
plain_explanation: Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture says that in the group algebra of a torsion-free group, two nonzero elements can never multiply to zero. This disproves it over the field with two elements.

subject: Algebra
title: A torsion-free group algebra that is not directly finite
plain_explanation: This disproves Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture ("ab = 1 implies ba = 1" in group algebras) in characteristic 2 and in odd characteristic. The group used is non-sofic, which also settles the long-open question of whether non-sofic groups exist. Companion examples give an injective but non-surjective cellular automaton (disproving Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture) and disprove the group-ring determinant conjecture.

subject: Algebra
title: A counterexample to finitistic-dimension finiteness
plain_explanation: The little finitistic dimension conjecture is disproved: this gives a finite-dimensional algebra whose modules have unboundedly large finite projective dimensions.

subject: Algebra
title: Counterexamples to Auslander–Reiten, Tachikawa and related homological conjectures
plain_explanation: This gives finite-dimensional algebras that disprove the Auslander–Reiten conjecture, Tachikawa's second conjecture and, via an associated algebra, the classical, generalized and strong Nakayama conjectures, plus related homological conjectures.

subject: Algebra
title: Eisenbud–Green–Harris and lex-plus-powers
plain_explanation: The Eisenbud–Green–Harris and lex-plus-powers conjectures (on the possible sizes and syzygies of polynomial ideals containing a regular sequence) are proven over every characteristic-zero field.

subject: Algebra
title: A counterexample to Kurosh’s division-ring problem
plain_explanation: Kurosh's problem for division rings: this builds a division ring that is algebraic over its centre and generated by two elements, yet infinite-dimensional over its centre.

subject: Algebra
title: The blockwise Alperin weight conjecture
